trials.toxicity: Grade ≥3 adverse events 88.9% vs 88.2%; atrial fibrillation 6.7% vs 4.4%, against 13.9% with ibrutinib in SHINE; grade 5 COVID-19 9.4% vs 6.7%
trials.reference: Wang M et al. JCO 2025;43:2276
highlights: Led to approval of acalabrutinib with bendamustine-rituximab for untreated transplant-ineligible mantle cell
Half the atrial fibrillation of ibrutinib, but still no survival benefit
Ran through the pandemic — COVID deaths materially blunted both curves, hence the prespecified censored analysis
trials.takeaway: Acalabrutinib with bendamustine-rituximab extends PFS to 66 months in older mantle cell with less cardiac toxicity than ibrutinib.

trials.name: PROPEL (pralatrexate)
trials.descriptor: single-arm pivotal study of pralatrexate in relapsed or refractory peripheral T-cell lymphoma
trials.population: 115 enrolled and 109 evaluable with independently confirmed PTCL progressing after at least one prior therapy; median 3 prior systemic regimens (range 1-12), 70% had failed CHOP, PTCL-NOS in 53%
trials.arms: Single arm — pralatrexate 30 mg/m² IV weekly for 6 of every 7 weeks, with B12 and folate supplementation
trials.primary_endpoint: Overall response rate by independent central review
trials.results: ORR 29% with complete response 11% and partial response 18%. Median duration of response 10.1 months, median PFS 3.5 months, median OS 14.5 months. Response was independent of age, histology, number of prior therapies, prior methotrexate or prior transplant
trials.toxicity: Grade 3-4 thrombocytopenia 32%, mucositis 22%, neutropenia 22%, anemia 18%
trials.reference: O'Connor OA et al. JCO 2011;29:1182
highlights: The first drug ever approved for relapsed peripheral T-cell lymphoma
Responses are infrequent at 29% but durable at 10.1 months; median PFS of 3.5 months shows how fast non-responders progress
Mucositis is the signature toxicity and mandates B12 and folate support
Not to be confused with PROpel in prostate cancer (olaparib + abiraterone) — unrelated trials with near-identical names
trials.takeaway: Pralatrexate produces durable but infrequent responses in heavily pretreated PTCL and was the first agent approved for the disease.

trials.name: BELIEF (CLN-19)
trials.descriptor: single-arm pivotal study of belinostat in relapsed or refractory PTCL
trials.population: 129 enrolled and 120 evaluable with confirmed PTCL progressing after at least one prior therapy; median 2 prior regimens
trials.arms: Single arm — belinostat 1,000 mg/m² as a 30-minute infusion on days 1-5 every 21 days
trials.primary_endpoint: Overall response rate by central assessment
trials.results: ORR 25.8% with complete response 10.8%. Median duration of response 13.6 months, but median PFS only 1.6 months and median OS 7.9 months. Twelve patients were bridged to stem cell transplant
trials.toxicity: Notably mild for the class — grade 3-4 anemia 10.8%, thrombocytopenia 7%, neutropenia 6.2%
trials.reference: O'Connor OA et al. JCO 2015;33:2492
highlights: A quarter of patients respond, and those who do respond for over a year — the median PFS of 1.6 months reflects how sharply responders and non-responders diverge
Low myelosuppression makes it useful as a bridge to transplant
trials.takeaway: Belinostat produces responses in about a quarter of relapsed PTCL patients, and those responses last more than a year.

trials.name: ALCANZA
trials.descriptor: brentuximab vedotin vs physician's choice of methotrexate or bexarotene in mycosis fungoides or primary cutaneous ALCL
trials.population: 131 randomized with CD30-positive (≥10%) mycosis fungoides or primary cutaneous ALCL, previously treated, at 52 centres in 13 countries; median 2 prior systemic therapies
trials.arms: Brentuximab vedotin 1.8 mg/kg q3wk up to 16 cycles vs physician's choice of methotrexate 5-50 mg weekly or bexarotene 300 mg/m² daily for up to 48 weeks
trials.primary_endpoint: ORR4 — objective global response lasting at least 4 months, by independent review. Not plain response rate
trials.results: ORR4 56.3% vs 12.5%, difference 43.8 points (29.1-58.4), P<0.0001. Median PFS 16.7 vs 3.5 months. At final analysis, complete response 17.2% vs 1.6% and time to next treatment 14.2 vs 5.6 months
trials.toxicity: Peripheral neuropathy in 67% vs 6%, mostly reversible with 86% resolved or improved; discontinuation for adverse events 24% vs 8%
trials.reference: Prince HM et al. Lancet 2017;390:555
highlights: The first randomized phase 3 of a new agent against standard of care in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
The endpoint is ORR4, which builds durability into the response definition
Neuropathy in two thirds of patients is the dominant, if reversible, cost
trials.takeaway: Brentuximab vedotin quadrupled durable response rates over methotrexate or bexarotene in CD30-positive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

trials.name: MAVORIC
trials.descriptor: mogamulizumab vs vorinostat in relapsed or refractory mycosis fungoides and Sezary syndrome
trials.population: 372 randomized with relapsed or refractory mycosis fungoides or Sezary syndrome after at least one prior systemic therapy, ECOG ≤1, at 61 centres in 11 countries
trials.arms: Mogamulizumab 1.0 mg/kg IV weekly for cycle 1 then days 1 and 15 vs vorinostat 400 mg orally daily; open-label with crossover permitted
trials.results: Median PFS 7.7 months (5.7-10.3) vs 3.1 months (2.9-4.1), HR 0.53 (0.41-0.69), P<0.0001. A total of 135 patients crossed over from vorinostat
trials.toxicity: Grade 3-4 adverse events 41% in both arms. Mogamulizumab: infusion reactions 33.2%, drug eruption 23.9%. Vorinostat: diarrhea 55.4%, nausea 38.2%
trials.reference: Kim YH et al. Lancet Oncol 2018;19:1192
highlights: The registrational trial for mogamulizumab, with the strongest effect in Sezary syndrome and B2 blood involvement
Mogamulizumab-associated rash is both a signature toxicity and, confusingly, a marker of response
trials.takeaway: Mogamulizumab more than doubled PFS over vorinostat in previously treated mycosis fungoides and Sezary syndrome.

trials.name: ECHELON-2
trials.descriptor: brentuximab vedotin + CHP vs CHOP in CD30-positive peripheral T-cell lymphoma
trials.population: 452 patients with untreated CD30-positive PTCL (≥10% CD30), 70% of them systemic ALCL; 78% had IPI ≥2
trials.arms: Brentuximab vedotin 1.8 mg/kg + cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin and prednisone vs CHOP, 6-8 cycles, double-blind
trials.primary_endpoint: Progression-free survival by blinded independent central review
trials.results: Median PFS 48.2 vs 20.8 months, HR 0.71 (0.54-0.93), P=0.0110. Overall survival HR 0.66 (0.46-0.95), P=0.0244 — the first regimen to beat CHOP on survival in PTCL. At five years, PFS 51.4% vs 43.0% and OS 70.1% vs 61.0%
trials.toxicity: Comparable to CHOP overall; peripheral neuropathy resolved or improved in 72%
trials.reference: Horwitz S et al. Lancet 2019;393:229
highlights: The only frontline regimen to improve both PFS and overall survival over CHOP in PTCL
Seventy percent of enrollment was systemic ALCL by design, so it is not powered for other subtypes — the AITL subgroup numerically favored CHOP
trials.takeaway: BV-CHP is the frontline standard for CD30-positive PTCL, especially systemic ALCL, on the strength of both PFS and survival.

trials.name: CALGB 9221
trials.descriptor: azacitidine vs supportive care, first HMA RCT
trials.population: MDS (higher- and lower-risk FAB subtypes)
trials.arms: Azacitidine (75 mg/m²/day SC ×7 days q28d) vs best supportive care (crossover allowed)
trials.results: Higher response (~60% vs 5%) and delayed transformation to AML/death; improved quality of life (OS not significant — crossover)
trials.reference: Silverman LR et al. JCO 2002;20:2429
highlights: The first RCT of azacitidine in MDS → the disease-modifying signal that led to FDA approval (2004).
trials.takeaway: First azacitidine RCT — response and delayed AML transformation; led to FDA approval

trials.name: D-0007
trials.descriptor: Decitabine added to supportive care vs supportive care alone
trials.population: 170 adults with de novo or secondary MDS (IPSS Int-1, Int-2 or high risk); ~70% IPSS Int-2/high risk; CMML included
trials.arms: Decitabine 15 mg/m2 IV over 3 h every 8 h x 3 days (135 mg/m2 per course) every 6 weeks + supportive care vs best supportive care alone
trials.primary_endpoint: Overall response rate (IWG) and time to AML transformation or death
trials.results: ORR 17% with decitabine (9% CR, 8% PR) vs 0% with supportive care (P<.001); a further 13% had hematologic improvement. Median response duration 10.3 months. Time to AML progression or death favored decitabine but was not significant overall: 12.1 vs 7.8 months (P=.16); significant only in subgroups (IPSS Int-2/high 12.0 vs 6.8 months, P=.03). No overall survival benefit was demonstrated. Median exposure was only 3 courses because the protocol withdrew patients after a maintained CR or after 6-8 cycles without response.
trials.toxicity: Myelosuppression: grade 3-4 neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and febrile neutropenia; serious adverse events in 69% of decitabine-treated patients.
trials.reference: Kantarjian H et al. Cancer 2006;106:1794-803
highlights: The registration trial that won decitabine FDA approval for MDS in 2006 - it established response and delayed AML transformation, not survival.

Cycle number was capped by protocol design (median 3 courses), the standard explanation for why decitabine underperformed azacitidine; modern practice is at least 4-6 cycles before declaring HMA failure.
trials.takeaway: Decitabine produced real responses (ORR 17% vs 0%) and delayed AML transformation in higher-risk subgroups, but showed no overall survival benefit - in contrast to azacitidine in AZA-001.

trials.name: MDS-003
trials.descriptor: lenalidomide, lower-risk del(5q) MDS
trials.population: Lower/Int-1-risk, transfusion-dependent MDS with del(5q)
trials.arms: Single-arm phase 2 (lenalidomide 10 mg/day)
trials.results: 67% transfusion independence; 73% cytogenetic response (45% complete)
trials.reference: List AF et al. NEJM 2006;355:1456
highlights: Established lenalidomide for transfusion-dependent lower-risk del(5q) MDS (FDA approval).
trials.takeaway: Lenalidomide → 67% transfusion independence in lower-risk del(5q) MDS

trials.name: AZA-001
trials.descriptor: azacitidine, higher-risk MDS survival benefit
trials.population: Higher-risk MDS (IPSS Int-2/High; RAEB)
trials.arms: Azacitidine vs conventional care regimens (supportive care, low-dose cytarabine, or intensive chemo — physician's choice)
trials.results: Median OS 24.5 vs 15.0 months (HR 0.58, p<0.001)
trials.reference: Fenaux P et al. Lancet Oncol 2009;10:223
highlights: The practice-defining trial: first to show a survival benefit for a hypomethylating agent in higher-risk MDS.
trials.takeaway: Azacitidine improves OS in higher-risk MDS (24.5 vs 15.0 mo)

trials.name: EORTC 06011
trials.setting: Higher-risk MDS in older adults ineligible for intensive chemotherapy, first line
trials.descriptor: Low-dose decitabine vs best supportive care, powered for overall survival
trials.population: 233 patients age >=60 (median 70) with primary or secondary MDS or CMML, IPSS intermediate or high risk, ineligible for intensive chemotherapy; 53% poor-risk cytogenetics
trials.arms: Decitabine 15 mg/m2 IV over 4 h three times daily x 3 days in 6-week cycles (max 8 cycles) vs best supportive care
trials.results: Primary endpoint NOT met: median OS 10.1 vs 8.5 months, HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.66-1.17), P=.38 - no overall survival benefit, in contrast to azacitidine in AZA-001. PFS was prolonged: 6.6 vs 3.0 months, HR 0.68 (0.52-0.88), P=.004. AML-free survival not significant: 8.8 vs 6.1 months, P=.24. AML transformation at 1 year 22% vs 33% (P=.036). CR 13% vs 0%, PR 6% vs 0%, HI 15% vs 2%. Patients received a median of only 4 cycles and ~40% received no more than 2.
trials.toxicity: Grade 3-4 febrile neutropenia 25% vs 7%; grade 3-4 infections 57% vs 52%.
trials.reference: Lubbert M et al. J Clin Oncol 2011;29:1987-96
highlights: The definitive OS-powered test of decitabine against supportive care in higher-risk MDS - and it was negative, which is why azacitidine, not decitabine, is the HMA with a proven survival benefit.
Decitabine still delayed progression and AML transformation and improved quality of life, so it remains reasonable when schedule or tolerability favors it.
trials.takeaway: In older higher-risk MDS, decitabine improved PFS, response and AML transformation but did NOT improve overall survival (10.1 vs 8.5 months, HR 0.88, P=.38) - the key contrast with AZA-001.

trials.name: MDS-004
trials.setting: Lower-risk del(5q) MDS with RBC transfusion dependence
trials.descriptor: Lenalidomide at two dose schedules vs placebo for transfusion independence
trials.population: 205 RBC transfusion-dependent patients with IPSS Low- or Intermediate-1-risk del(5q31) MDS
trials.arms: Lenalidomide 10 mg/day days 1-21 (n=69) vs 5 mg/day days 1-28 (n=69) vs placebo (n=67), 28-day cycles; crossover permitted after 16 weeks
trials.results: RBC-TI >=26 weeks 56.1% (10 mg) and 42.6% (5 mg) vs 5.9% (placebo), both P<.001. Cytogenetic response 50.0% vs 25.0% (P=.066). Pooled lenalidomide 3-year OS 56.5%, 3-year AML risk 25.1%. Achieving RBC-TI >=8 weeks was associated with a 47% reduction in relative risk of death (P=.021) and 42% reduction in risk of AML progression or death (P=.048).
trials.toxicity: Myelosuppression dominates - grade 3-4 neutropenia and thrombocytopenia requiring dose reduction and interruption.
trials.reference: Fenaux P et al. Blood 2011;118:3765-76
highlights: The randomized placebo-controlled confirmation of lenalidomide in del(5q) MDS, establishing 10 mg days 1-21 as the standard schedule.
Achieving transfusion independence was itself associated with lower risk of death and of AML progression - TI is more than a cosmetic endpoint.
trials.takeaway: Lenalidomide 10 mg (days 1-21) makes roughly half of transfusion-dependent lower-risk del(5q) patients transfusion independent for >=26 weeks, at the cost of significant myelosuppression.

trials.name: MEDALIST
trials.descriptor: luspatercept, lower-risk RS+ MDS after ESA failure
trials.population: Lower-risk, transfusion-dependent MDS with ring sideroblasts / SF3B1, ESA-refractory or -ineligible
trials.arms: Luspatercept vs placebo
trials.results: 38% vs 13% achieved transfusion independence ≥8 wk
trials.reference: Fenaux P et al. NEJM 2020;382:140
highlights: Luspatercept (activin receptor II ligand trap) for RS+ lower-risk MDS after ESA failure (FDA approval).
trials.takeaway: Luspatercept → transfusion independence in RS+ lower-risk MDS after ESA failure

trials.name: BMT CTN 1102
trials.descriptor: Biologic assignment to reduced-intensity allogeneic HCT (donor) vs non-transplant therapy (no donor)
trials.population: 384 patients age 50-75 with de novo MDS that was or had been IPSS Intermediate-2 or high risk; <20% marrow blasts; suitable RIC alloHCT candidates; 34 centers, 2014-2018
trials.arms: Donor arm: reduced-intensity conditioning allogeneic HCT. No-Donor arm: hypomethylating therapy or best supportive care. Assignment was biologic - by availability of an HLA-matched related or unrelated donor within 90 days - not randomized
trials.results: Adjusted 3-year overall survival 47.9% (95% CI 41.3-54.1) in the Donor arm vs 26.6% (95% CI 18.4-35.6) in the No-Donor arm, P=.0001; absolute difference 21.3% (95% CI 10.2-31.8). Three-year leukemia-free survival 35.8% vs 20.6%, P=.003. Benefit seen across all subgroups examined.
trials.reference: Nakamura R et al. J Clin Oncol 2021;39:3328-3339
highlights: The best available evidence that reduced-intensity allogeneic transplant should be offered to fit older adults with higher-risk MDS - a 21-point absolute gain in 3-year survival.
Assignment was by donor availability rather than randomization, which avoids the selection bias of retrospective transplant series while stopping short of a true randomized comparison.
trials.takeaway: Fit patients aged 50-75 with higher-risk MDS who have a matched donor and proceed to RIC allogeneic HCT live substantially longer (3-year OS 47.9% vs 26.6%) - start the donor search at diagnosis.

trials.name: COMMANDS
trials.descriptor: luspatercept vs epoetin alfa, first-line lower-risk MDS
trials.population: Lower-risk, transfusion-dependent MDS, ESA-naive
trials.arms: Luspatercept vs epoetin alfa (head-to-head, first-line)
trials.primary_endpoint: Transfusion independence ≥12 wk + mean Hb rise ≥1.5 g/dL
trials.results: Luspatercept superior: ~59% vs ~31%
trials.reference: Platzbecker U et al. Lancet 2023;402:373
highlights: Moved luspatercept to first-line for transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS (beat ESA), regardless of ring-sideroblast status.
trials.takeaway: Luspatercept beats epoetin alfa first-line in transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS

trials.name: IMerge
trials.descriptor: imetelstat, lower-risk MDS after ESA failure
trials.population: Lower-risk, transfusion-dependent MDS, relapsed/refractory to ESAs, non-del(5q)
trials.arms: Imetelstat (telomerase inhibitor) vs placebo
trials.results: 40% vs 15% (8-wk TI); durable responses
trials.reference: Platzbecker U et al. Lancet 2024;403:249
highlights: Imetelstat (first-in-class telomerase inhibitor) for ESA-failed lower-risk MDS; FDA-approved 2024 (Rytelo).
trials.takeaway: Imetelstat — telomerase inhibitor for ESA-failed lower-risk MDS (TI 40% vs 15%)

trials.name: VERONA
trials.setting: Treatment-naive intermediate- and higher-risk MDS, first line
trials.descriptor: Adding venetoclax to azacitidine in newly diagnosed higher-risk MDS
trials.population: 509 randomized patients with newly diagnosed MDS, <20% marrow blasts, IPSS-R >3 (intermediate, high or very high); median age 72; prior HMA, therapy-related MDS, MDS/MPN and CMML excluded
trials.arms: Venetoclax 400 mg PO daily days 1-14 + azacitidine 75 mg/m2 on 7 of the first 9 days (n=256) vs placebo + identical azacitidine (n=253), 28-day cycles
trials.results: Primary endpoint NOT met: median OS 22.18 months (95% CI 17.28-27.27) vs 21.68 months (95% CI 17.81-23.79); HR 0.908 (95% CI 0.733-1.126), P=.38 at median follow-up 41.2 months. Secondary endpoints favored the combination: modified ORR 76.2% vs 57.7%; marrow CR 57.8% vs 37.5%; transfusion independence 55.7% vs 33.6% (P=.0003). Subgroup signals in >5% to <20% marrow blasts and in ASXL1, TP53 or RUNX1 mutated disease.
trials.toxicity: No new safety signals. Neutropenia 77.3% vs 60.2%, thrombocytopenia 66.3% vs 58.9%. Dose interruption 78.8% vs 67.9%; azacitidine dose reduction 48.6% vs 27.2%.
trials.reference: Garcia-Manero G et al. SOHO Annual Meeting 2025; abstract MDS-1497
highlights: The largest randomized test of venetoclax in higher-risk MDS - deeper marrow responses and more transfusion independence, but no survival gain, so azacitidine monotherapy remains the standard first-line HMA.
The dissociation between marrow response and survival is the lesson: in MDS, unlike AML, adding venetoclax to an HMA improves depth of response without translating into longer life.
trials.takeaway: Venetoclax added to azacitidine did not prolong overall survival in treatment-naive higher-risk MDS (22.18 vs 21.68 months, HR 0.908, P=.38) despite much higher response rates - not a new standard of care.

trials.name: CheckMate 067
trials.descriptor: nivolumab + ipilimumab vs nivolumab vs ipilimumab
trials.population: Untreated unresectable stage III or IV melanoma
trials.arms: Nivolumab 1 mg/kg + ipilimumab 3 mg/kg × 4 → nivolumab vs nivolumab alone vs ipilimumab alone
trials.primary_endpoint: PFS and OS (combination or nivolumab vs ipilimumab)
trials.results: Primary: PFS 11.5 / 6.9 / 2.9 mo. 10-yr: median OS 72.1 / 36.9 / 19.9 mo; 10-yr OS 43% / 37% / 19%; 10-yr melanoma-specific survival 52% / 44% / 23%; patients progression-free at 3 years had >96% 10-yr MSS
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 treatment-related AEs 59% (combo) vs 24% (nivo) vs 28% (ipi)
trials.reference: Larkin J et al. NEJM 2015;373:23; Wolchok JD et al. NEJM 2025;392:11 (10-yr)
highlights: Ipi/nivo gives the longest survival — roughly half of patients alive at 10 years — at the cost of ~60% grade 3–4 immune toxicity.
Being progression-free at 3 years essentially equals cure; guides the length of surveillance conversations.
trials.takeaway: Nivolumab + ipilimumab yields ~50% 10-year melanoma-specific survival in metastatic melanoma

trials.name: DeCOG-SLT
trials.descriptor: completion lymph node dissection vs observation after positive sentinel node (German trial)
trials.population: Melanoma with sentinel-node metastasis (≤1 mm micrometastasis in 66%), trunk or extremity primary
trials.arms: Complete lymph node dissection vs observation with nodal ultrasound q3mo
trials.results: 3-yr DMFS 77.0% vs 74.9% (NS); 5-yr DMFS, RFS and OS all equivalent; regional recurrence similar
trials.reference: Leiter U et al. Lancet Oncol 2016;17:757; JCO 2019;37:3000 (final)
highlights: With MSLT-II, retired routine completion dissection after a positive sentinel node — nodal ultrasound surveillance is the standard.
Applies mostly to low sentinel-node tumor burden; heavy nodal disease is now managed with neoadjuvant immunotherapy (NADINA).
trials.takeaway: Completion node dissection does not improve DMFS or OS after positive sentinel node (with MSLT-II)

trials.name: CheckMate 238
trials.descriptor: adjuvant nivolumab vs ipilimumab, resected stage IIIB/C–IV
trials.population: Completely resected stage IIIB, IIIC or IV melanoma
trials.arms: Nivolumab 3 mg/kg q2wk vs ipilimumab 10 mg/kg q3wk × 4 then q12wk, each × 1 year
trials.results: 12-mo RFS 70.5% vs 60.8% (HR 0.65); 5-yr RFS 50% vs 39%; 5-yr OS 76% vs 72% (NS); grade 3–4 AEs 14% vs 46%
trials.reference: Weber J et al. NEJM 2017;377:1824; Larkin J et al. Clin Cancer Res 2023 (5-yr)
highlights: Nivolumab beat high-dose ipilimumab on efficacy and toxicity — the trial that retired adjuvant ipilimumab.
Extends adjuvant anti-PD-1 to resected stage IV disease.
trials.takeaway: Adjuvant nivolumab beats ipilimumab for RFS with a third of the toxicity in resected stage III–IV melanoma

trials.name: COMBI-AD
trials.descriptor: adjuvant dabrafenib + trametinib, resected stage III BRAF V600E/K
trials.population: Completely resected stage III melanoma with BRAF V600E or V600K mutation
trials.arms: Dabrafenib 150 mg BID + trametinib 2 mg daily × 12 months vs placebo
trials.results: 3-yr RFS 58% vs 39% (HR 0.47); 5-yr RFS 52% vs 36% (HR 0.51); DMFS HR 0.55; OS HR 0.80 (10-yr update, 2024; did not reach significance threshold)
trials.toxicity: Pyrexia (63%), fatigue, nausea; 26% discontinued for AEs
trials.reference: Long GV et al. NEJM 2017;377:1813; Dummer R et al. NEJM 2020 (5-yr)
highlights: The targeted-therapy alternative to anti-PD-1 for resected BRAF-mutant stage III — durable RFS benefit with a plateau after year 3.
Choose vs anti-PD-1 on toxicity profile and patient preference; no head-to-head trial.
trials.takeaway: 12 months of adjuvant dabrafenib + trametinib halves relapse risk in resected BRAF V600 stage III melanoma

trials.name: MSLT-II
trials.descriptor: completion lymph node dissection vs observation after positive sentinel node
trials.population: Melanoma with sentinel-node metastasis
trials.arms: Immediate completion lymph node dissection vs nodal observation with ultrasound
trials.results: 3-yr melanoma-specific survival 86% vs 86% (HR 1.08, NS); regional control better with CLND (92% vs 77%) but no survival benefit; lymphedema 24% vs 6%
trials.reference: Faries MB et al. NEJM 2017;376:2211
highlights: Completion dissection after a positive sentinel node improves regional control but not survival — ultrasound surveillance is now standard (with DeCOG-SLT).
SLNB remains valuable for staging and adjuvant-therapy eligibility.
trials.takeaway: Completion node dissection after positive SLNB does not improve melanoma-specific survival

trials.name: CheckMate 204
trials.descriptor: nivolumab + ipilimumab for melanoma brain metastases
trials.population: Melanoma with ≥1 measurable, untreated brain metastasis (0.5–3 cm); cohort A asymptomatic without steroids, cohort B symptomatic or on steroids
trials.arms: Single-arm: nivolumab 1 mg/kg + ipilimumab 3 mg/kg × 4 → nivolumab 3 mg/kg q2wk
trials.results: Asymptomatic: intracranial ORR 53–57%, 36-mo intracranial PFS ~54%, OS ~72%. Symptomatic/steroids: ORR ~17–22%, 36-mo iPFS ~19%, OS ~37%
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 AEs 55%; CNS events (headache, edema) in ~7%
trials.reference: Tawbi HA et al. NEJM 2018;379:722; Long GV et al. JCO 2023 (3-yr)
highlights: Asymptomatic, steroid-free brain metastases respond to ipi/nivo about as well as extracranial disease — upfront systemic therapy is appropriate, with SRS reserved for residual/oligo lesions.
Steroid dependence is the discriminator: symptomatic patients do poorly on IO and need local therapy ± BRAF/MEK first.
trials.takeaway: Ipi/nivo controls asymptomatic melanoma brain metastases (intracranial ORR >50%); steroid-requiring patients respond poorly

trials.name: KEYNOTE-054 (EORTC 1325)
trials.descriptor: adjuvant pembrolizumab, resected stage III
trials.population: Completely resected stage IIIA (>1 mm nodal metastasis), IIIB or IIIC melanoma
trials.arms: Pembrolizumab 200 mg q3wk × 18 vs placebo (crossover to pembrolizumab at recurrence)
trials.results: 1-yr RFS 75.4% vs 61.0% (HR 0.57); 5-yr RFS 55.4% vs 38.3% (HR 0.61); 5-yr DMFS 60.6% vs 44.5% (HR 0.62); benefit regardless of PD-L1 or BRAF status; OS not significant (crossover)
trials.toxicity: Grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs 14.7%; endocrinopathies
trials.reference: Eggermont AMM et al. NEJM 2018;378:1789; Lancet Oncol 2021 / NEJM Evidence 2022 (5-yr)
highlights: Established adjuvant anti-PD-1 as the standard for resected stage III melanoma, replacing high-dose ipilimumab and interferon.
Now being partly displaced by neoadjuvant IO (NADINA) for macroscopic nodal disease.
trials.takeaway: Adjuvant pembrolizumab improves RFS and DMFS in resected stage III melanoma

trials.name: KEYNOTE-716
trials.descriptor: adjuvant pembrolizumab, resected stage IIB/IIC
trials.population: Completely resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma (node-negative, sentinel biopsy negative)
trials.arms: Pembrolizumab 200 mg q3wk × 17 vs placebo
trials.results: 12-mo RFS 90.5% vs 83.1% (HR 0.65 at first interim; 0.61 at second); 3-yr RFS 76.2% vs 63.4% (HR 0.62); DMFS HR 0.59; OS not yet significant
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 treatment-related AEs 17%; permanent endocrinopathies (hypothyroidism ~17%)
trials.reference: Luke JJ et al. Lancet 2022;399:1718; Long GV et al. Lancet Oncol 2023 (DMFS)
highlights: Extends adjuvant anti-PD-1 to node-negative high-risk primaries — RFS and DMFS benefit, but no OS benefit yet, so the conversation is about risk tolerance and irreversible endocrine toxicity.
Stage IIB/IIC recurrence risk rivals stage IIIA/B; SLNB-negative does not mean low risk.
trials.takeaway: Adjuvant pembrolizumab improves RFS and DMFS in resected stage IIB/IIC melanoma (no OS benefit yet)

trials.name: RELATIVITY-047
trials.descriptor: nivolumab + relatlimab (anti-LAG-3) vs nivolumab
trials.population: Untreated unresectable or metastatic melanoma
trials.arms: Nivolumab 480 mg + relatlimab 160 mg q4wk (fixed-dose combination) vs nivolumab 480 mg
trials.results: PFS 10.1 vs 4.6 mo (HR 0.75); OS HR 0.80 (NS at analysis); ORR 43% vs 33%
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 treatment-related AEs 19% vs 10% (far below ipi/nivo); adrenal insufficiency and myocarditis slightly increased
trials.reference: Tawbi HA et al. NEJM 2022;386:24
highlights: First LAG-3 inhibitor to reach the clinic (Opdualag) — doubles PFS over nivolumab with roughly a third of ipi/nivo's grade 3–4 toxicity.
Reasonable first-line default when ipi/nivo toxicity is a concern; no direct comparison with ipi/nivo exists, and OS benefit was not significant.
trials.takeaway: Nivolumab + relatlimab doubles PFS over nivolumab alone with modest added toxicity

trials.name: CheckMate 76K
trials.descriptor: adjuvant nivolumab, resected stage IIB/IIC
trials.population: Completely resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma
trials.arms: Nivolumab 480 mg q4wk × 12 months vs placebo
trials.results: 12-mo RFS 89% vs 79% (HR 0.42); DMFS HR 0.47; 3-yr RFS HR 0.62 (updated)
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 treatment-related AEs 10%
trials.reference: Kirkwood JM et al. Nat Med 2023;29:2835
highlights: Nivolumab is the alternative to pembrolizumab for stage IIB/IIC; same caveat — no OS benefit demonstrated yet.
trials.takeaway: Adjuvant nivolumab reduces recurrence in resected stage IIB/IIC melanoma

trials.name: DREAMseq (ECOG-ACRIN EA6134)
trials.descriptor: immunotherapy-first vs targeted-first sequencing in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma
trials.population: Untreated BRAF V600-mutant metastatic melanoma (asymptomatic brain mets allowed)
trials.arms: Ipilimumab + nivolumab → dabrafenib + trametinib at progression vs dabrafenib + trametinib → ipilimumab + nivolumab
trials.results: 2-yr OS 71.8% vs 51.5% (IO-first vs targeted-first); trial stopped early for benefit; ORR to first-line IO 46%, to first-line BRAF/MEK 43%
trials.reference: Atkins MB et al. JCO 2023;41:186
highlights: Start with immunotherapy in BRAF-mutant disease — the survival difference comes from durability of IO responses and the poor activity of IO after BRAF/MEK failure.
Exceptions: visceral crisis, symptomatic disease or steroid dependence, where a short BRAF/MEK 'sandwich' buys control first.
trials.takeaway: Ipi/nivo first then BRAF/MEK beats the reverse sequence for OS in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma

trials.name: SECOMBIT
trials.descriptor: sequencing: targeted-first vs IO-first vs 'sandwich' in BRAF-mutant melanoma
trials.population: Untreated BRAF V600-mutant metastatic melanoma
trials.arms: Arm A: encorafenib + binimetinib → ipi/nivo; Arm B: ipi/nivo → encorafenib + binimetinib; Arm C 'sandwich': 8 weeks enco/bini → ipi/nivo → enco/bini at progression
trials.results: 2-yr OS 65% (A, targeted-first) / 73% (B, IO-first) / 69% (C, sandwich); 3-yr OS 54% / 62% / 60%; median OS not reached in any arm; longer follow-up (ASCO 2024 update) continued to favor IO-first and sandwich for PFS and OS
trials.reference: Ascierto PA et al. JCO 2023;41:212
highlights: Concordant with DREAMseq: IO-first or a brief targeted 'sandwich' beats targeted-first for long-term survival.
The sandwich strategy is the evidence base for using BRAF/MEK briefly to debulk symptomatic disease before switching to IO.
trials.takeaway: IO-first or brief targeted 'sandwich' outperforms targeted-first sequencing for OS in BRAF-mutant melanoma

trials.name: SWOG S1801
trials.descriptor: neoadjuvant-adjuvant vs adjuvant-only pembrolizumab
trials.population: Resectable stage IIIB–IV melanoma (measurable disease)
trials.arms: Pembrolizumab 200 mg × 3 pre-op → surgery → 15 adjuvant doses vs surgery → 18 adjuvant doses (same total)
trials.results: 2-yr EFS 72% vs 49% (HR 0.58); no increase in surgical complications; same total pembrolizumab exposure
trials.reference: Patel SP et al. NEJM 2023;388:813
highlights: Proof that the timing of immunotherapy matters: three doses before surgery, with the tumor and its draining nodes in place, outperform the identical total dose given afterward.
Foundation for NADINA and for neoadjuvant IO as the default in resectable stage III disease.
trials.takeaway: Giving 3 of 18 pembrolizumab doses before surgery improves EFS vs the same doses all after surgery

trials.name: NADINA
trials.descriptor: neoadjuvant ipilimumab + nivolumab vs adjuvant nivolumab, macroscopic stage III
trials.population: Resectable macroscopic stage III melanoma (≥1 pathologically proven lymph node metastasis)
trials.arms: Neoadjuvant ipilimumab 80 mg + nivolumab 240 mg × 2 → TLND; adjuvant nivolumab only if no major pathologic response (or dab/tram if BRAF+) vs upfront TLND → adjuvant nivolumab × 12
trials.results: 12-mo EFS 83.7% vs 57.2% (HR 0.32); major pathologic response 59%; those with MPR had 12-mo RFS 95% — most avoided adjuvant therapy
trials.toxicity: Grade ≥3 systemic AEs 29.7% (neoadjuvant) vs 14.7%
trials.reference: Blank CU et al. NEJM 2024;391:1696
highlights: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy is the new standard for macroscopic stage III melanoma — a huge EFS gain and a response-adapted de-escalation of adjuvant therapy.
The 'flipped' low-dose ipi (1 mg/kg) + nivo (3 mg/kg) × 2 keeps toxicity manageable before surgery.
trials.takeaway: Neoadjuvant ipi/nivo dramatically improves EFS over adjuvant nivolumab in resectable stage III melanoma

trials.name: CYTO-PV
trials.descriptor: hematocrit target <45% vs 45–50% in polycythemia vera
trials.population: JAK2-positive polycythemia vera treated with phlebotomy and/or hydroxyurea
trials.arms: Hematocrit target <45% (low) vs 45–50% (high)
trials.primary_endpoint: Time to cardiovascular death or major thrombosis
trials.results: Primary endpoint 2.7% vs 9.8% (HR 3.91 for the high-hematocrit target); more thromboses and CV events at 45–50%
trials.reference: Marchioli R et al. NEJM 2013;368:22
highlights: The number to defend: hematocrit <45% cuts cardiovascular death and major thrombosis roughly fourfold — phlebotomize or cytoreduce to hit it.
Applies to all PV patients regardless of risk category; iron replacement defeats the strategy.
trials.takeaway: Hematocrit target <45% cuts cardiovascular death and major thrombosis ~4-fold in PV

trials.name: RESPONSE
trials.descriptor: ruxolitinib vs best available therapy, hydroxyurea-resistant or -intolerant PV
trials.population: Polycythemia vera with splenomegaly, resistant or intolerant to hydroxyurea, phlebotomy-dependent
trials.arms: Ruxolitinib 10 mg BID vs best available therapy (crossover allowed)
trials.primary_endpoint: Composite of hematocrit control without phlebotomy + ≥35% spleen volume reduction at week 32
trials.results: Composite response 21% vs 1%; hematocrit control 60% vs 20%; spleen response 38% vs 1%; symptom improvement 49% vs 5%; thromboembolic events 1 vs 6
trials.toxicity: Anemia, thrombocytopenia, herpes zoster, non-melanoma skin cancer
trials.reference: Vannucchi AM et al. NEJM 2015;372:426
highlights: Ruxolitinib is the second-line option for PV after hydroxyurea failure — controls hematocrit, spleen and symptoms (FDA 2014).
Interferons (ropeginterferon) are now NCCN-preferred cytoreduction; ruxolitinib is for HU-resistant/intolerant disease.
trials.takeaway: Ruxolitinib controls hematocrit, spleen and symptoms in hydroxyurea-resistant/intolerant PV

trials.name: VERIFY
trials.descriptor: rusfertide (hepcidin mimetic) vs placebo, phlebotomy-dependent PV
trials.population: Polycythemia vera requiring frequent phlebotomy (≥3 in the prior 28 weeks) ± cytoreductive therapy
trials.arms: Rusfertide SQ weekly vs placebo, added to current therapy, × 32 weeks
trials.primary_endpoint: Proportion achieving clinical response (no phlebotomy eligibility) weeks 20–32
trials.results: Response 77% vs 33% (p<0.0001); mean phlebotomies 0.5 vs 1.8; hematocrit <45% maintained in 62% vs 15%; improved fatigue/symptom scores
trials.toxicity: Injection-site reactions, anemia rare; squamous skin cancers observed in phase 2 (monitored)
trials.reference: Kremyanskaya M et al. NEJM 2025 (ASCO/EHA 2025 plenary)
highlights: A hepcidin mimetic sequesters iron to hold hematocrit <45% without phlebotomy — addresses the iron deficiency that phlebotomy creates.
Regulatory decision pending; expected to be the first agent specifically for phlebotomy dependence in PV.
trials.takeaway: Rusfertide eliminates phlebotomy need in most phlebotomy-dependent PV patients (77% vs 33% response)

trials.name: PROMID
trials.descriptor: octreotide LAR vs placebo, metastatic midgut NET
trials.population: Treatment-naive, well-differentiated metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumors (functioning or non-functioning)
trials.arms: Octreotide LAR 30 mg IM q4wk vs placebo
trials.results: TTP 14.3 vs 6.0 mo (HR 0.34); stable disease at 6 mo 66.7% vs 37.2%; benefit greatest with low hepatic tumor burden (≤10%) and resected primary
trials.reference: Rinke A et al. JCO 2009;27:4656
highlights: First randomized proof that somatostatin analogues have antiproliferative (not just antisecretory) activity — octreotide LAR is first-line for metastatic midgut NET regardless of function.
Small trial stopped early; no OS benefit (crossover).
trials.takeaway: Octreotide LAR more than doubles time to progression in metastatic midgut NET

trials.name: RADIANT-3
trials.descriptor: everolimus vs placebo, advanced pancreatic NET
trials.population: Progressive, low- or intermediate-grade advanced pancreatic NET
trials.arms: Everolimus 10 mg daily vs placebo (SSA allowed)
trials.results: PFS 11.0 vs 4.6 mo (HR 0.35); ORR 5%; OS 44.0 vs 37.7 mo (NS, crossover)
trials.toxicity: Stomatitis, rash, diarrhea, hyperglycemia, pneumonitis
trials.reference: Yao JC et al. NEJM 2011;364:514; JCO 2016 (OS)
highlights: Established everolimus for pancreatic NET — disease stabilization rather than shrinkage.
Published alongside the sunitinib trial (Raymond, NEJM 2011); the two are the targeted-therapy options for pancreatic NET.
trials.takeaway: Everolimus more than doubles PFS in progressive pancreatic NET

trials.name: CLARINET
trials.descriptor: lanreotide vs placebo, non-functioning GEP-NET
trials.population: Advanced, non-functioning, well or moderately differentiated (Ki-67 <10%) GEP-NET, SSTR-positive; 96% had stable disease at baseline
trials.arms: Lanreotide autogel 120 mg SQ q4wk vs placebo
trials.results: PFS not reached vs 18.0 mo (HR 0.47); 24-mo PFS 65.1% vs 33.0%; open-label extension median PFS 38.5 mo
trials.reference: Caplin ME et al. NEJM 2014;371:224; Caplin ME et al. Endocr Relat Cancer 2016 (extension)
highlights: Extends the SSA antiproliferative effect to pancreatic NETs and Ki-67 up to 10% — lanreotide is first-line for metastatic SSTR-positive GEP-NET.
Most patients had stable disease at entry, so the trial speaks to delaying progression, not shrinking tumors.
trials.takeaway: Lanreotide halves the risk of progression in metastatic non-functioning GEP-NET

trials.name: RADIANT-4
trials.descriptor: everolimus vs placebo, non-functional lung or GI NET
trials.population: Progressive, well-differentiated, non-functional NET of lung or GI origin
trials.arms: Everolimus 10 mg daily vs placebo
trials.results: PFS 11.0 vs 3.9 mo (HR 0.48); ORR 2%; OS HR 0.64 (NS)
trials.reference: Yao JC et al. Lancet 2016;387:968
highlights: Extended everolimus to GI and lung NETs — the first targeted therapy approved for lung NET.
Excluded functional tumors; SSAs remain first-line for those.
trials.takeaway: Everolimus improves PFS in non-functional GI and lung NET

trials.name: NETTER-1
trials.descriptor: Lu-177 dotatate (PRRT) vs high-dose octreotide, progressive midgut NET
trials.population: Well-differentiated (G1–G2), SSTR-positive midgut NET progressing on standard-dose octreotide LAR
trials.arms: Lu-177 dotatate 7.4 GBq × 4 q8wk + octreotide LAR 30 mg vs octreotide LAR 60 mg q4wk
trials.results: 20-mo PFS 65.2% vs 10.8% (HR 0.21); median PFS not reached vs 8.4 mo; ORR 18% vs 3%; final OS 48.0 vs 36.3 mo (HR 0.84, NS, 36% crossover)
trials.toxicity: Nausea/vomiting during amino-acid infusion, lymphopenia; MDS/AML ~2%
trials.reference: Strosberg J et al. NEJM 2017;376:125; Strosberg JR et al. Lancet Oncol 2021 (OS)
highlights: Established PRRT for progressive SSTR-positive midgut NET (FDA 2018) with a 79% reduction in progression risk.
OS benefit was clinically meaningful (~12 months) but not statistically significant because of crossover.
trials.takeaway: Lu-177 dotatate dramatically improves PFS in progressive SSTR-positive midgut NET

trials.name: ECOG-ACRIN E2211 (CAPTEM)
trials.descriptor: capecitabine + temozolomide vs temozolomide alone, pancreatic NET
trials.population: Progressive, well-differentiated (G1–G2) advanced pancreatic NET
trials.arms: Capecitabine 750 mg/m² BID d1–14 + temozolomide 200 mg/m² d10–14 q28d vs temozolomide 200 mg/m² d1–5 q28d
trials.results: PFS 22.7 vs 14.4 mo (HR 0.58); ORR 40% vs 34%; OS 58.7 vs 53.8 mo (NS); MGMT deficiency associated with response but not required
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 AEs 45% vs 22%: cytopenias, nausea, fatigue
trials.reference: Kunz PL et al. JCO 2023;41:1359
highlights: CAPTEM is the chemotherapy of choice for pancreatic NET — the highest response rate among systemic options, useful when tumor shrinkage matters.
Activity is largely confined to pancreatic primaries; MGMT testing is not required to select patients.
trials.takeaway: Capecitabine + temozolomide improves PFS over temozolomide alone in pancreatic NET (22.7 vs 14.4 mo)

trials.name: CABINET (Alliance A021602)
trials.descriptor: cabozantinib vs placebo, previously treated pancreatic and extrapancreatic NET
trials.population: Progressive, well- or moderately-differentiated pancreatic NET (after ≥1 prior therapy) or extrapancreatic NET (after ≥1 prior FDA-approved therapy); two parallel cohorts
trials.arms: Cabozantinib 60 mg daily vs placebo
trials.results: Extrapancreatic: PFS 8.4 vs 3.9 mo (HR 0.38); pancreatic: PFS 13.8 vs 4.4 mo (HR 0.23); ORR 5% and 19%
trials.toxicity: Hypertension, fatigue, diarrhea, thromboembolic events; grade ≥3 AEs 62–65%
trials.reference: Chan JA et al. NEJM 2025;392:653 (ESMO 2023)
highlights: Cabozantinib is active in both pancreatic and extrapancreatic NET after prior therapy (including after PRRT and everolimus) — FDA-approved March 2025.
The first new agent for extrapancreatic (lung, GI) NET in a decade.
trials.takeaway: Cabozantinib improves PFS in previously treated pancreatic and extrapancreatic NET

trials.name: NETTER-2
trials.descriptor: first-line Lu-177 dotatate vs high-dose octreotide, higher-grade GEP-NET
trials.population: Newly diagnosed, SSTR-positive, well-differentiated G2 (Ki-67 10–20%) or G3 (Ki-67 21–55%) GEP-NET
trials.arms: Lu-177 dotatate × 4 + octreotide LAR 30 mg vs octreotide LAR 60 mg q4wk
trials.results: PFS 22.8 vs 8.5 mo (HR 0.28); ORR 43% vs 9%
trials.reference: Singh S et al. Lancet 2024;403:2807
highlights: First randomized trial of PRRT as first-line therapy and the first in G3 well-differentiated NET — high response rate where SSAs alone do little.
Not yet FDA-approved for this indication; COMPETE and other trials are testing PRRT against everolimus.
trials.takeaway: First-line Lu-177 dotatate nearly triples PFS in higher-grade (G2–G3) SSTR-positive GEP-NET

trials.name: COMPETE
trials.descriptor: Lu-177 edotreotide (PRRT) vs everolimus
trials.population: Progressive, SSTR-positive, well-differentiated G1–G2 GEP-NET (functioning or non-functioning)
trials.arms: Lu-177 edotreotide 7.5 GBq × 4 q3mo vs everolimus 10 mg daily
trials.results: PFS 23.9 vs 14.1 mo (HR 0.67); OS trending favorable but immature
trials.reference: Capdevila J et al. ENETS/ASCO 2025 (presented); publication pending
highlights: First head-to-head PRRT vs targeted therapy trial — PRRT wins on PFS, supporting PRRT before everolimus in SSTR-positive disease.
Uses a different ligand (edotreotide) than NETTER; the OS comparison is not yet significant.
trials.takeaway: Lu-177 edotreotide beats everolimus on PFS in progressive G1–G2 GEP-NET

trials.name: KEYNOTE-024
trials.descriptor: pembrolizumab monotherapy vs chemotherapy, PD-L1 ≥50%
trials.population: Untreated advanced NSCLC with PD-L1 TPS ≥50%, no EGFR/ALK alterations
trials.arms: Pembrolizumab 200 mg q3wk × 35 vs platinum doublet (crossover allowed)
trials.results: PFS 10.3 vs 6.0 mo (HR 0.50); OS 26.3 vs 13.4 mo (HR 0.62) despite 66% crossover; 5-yr OS 31.9% vs 16.3%
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–5 treatment-related AEs 31% vs 53%
trials.reference: Reck M et al. NEJM 2016;375:1823; JCO 2021 (5-yr)
highlights: Single-agent pembrolizumab is the standard for PD-L1 ≥50% without a driver — doubles OS vs chemo with less toxicity.
Established PD-L1 TPS ≥50% as the cutoff for chemo-free first-line immunotherapy.
trials.takeaway: Pembrolizumab alone doubles OS over chemotherapy first-line in PD-L1 ≥50% NSCLC

trials.name: AURA3
trials.descriptor: osimertinib vs chemo in T790M+ resistance
trials.population: Advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC with acquired T790M after progression on a 1st/2nd-gen EGFR TKI
trials.arms: Osimertinib vs platinum + pemetrexed
trials.results: PFS 10.1 vs 4.4 mo (HR 0.30); ORR 71% vs 31%; no OS difference (crossover)
trials.reference: Mok TS et al. NEJM 2017
highlights: Osimertinib's original indication — T790M-mediated resistance. Now historical, since osimertinib is used first-line (T790M no longer emerges as the dominant resistance mechanism).
trials.takeaway: Osimertinib beats chemo for T790M-positive resistance — its original indication, now historical

trials.name: PACIFIC
trials.descriptor: consolidation durvalumab after chemoradiation, unresectable stage III
trials.population: Unresectable stage III NSCLC without progression after ≥2 cycles of platinum-based concurrent chemoradiation (randomized within 42 days)
trials.arms: Durvalumab 10 mg/kg q2wk × 12 months vs placebo
trials.toxicity: Pneumonitis any grade 33.9% vs 24.8% (grade 3–4 similar, ~3–4%)
trials.reference: Antonia SJ et al. NEJM 2017;377:1919; NEJM 2018 (OS); Spigel DR et al. JCO 2022 (5-yr)
highlights: Consolidation durvalumab after chemoRT is the standard for unresectable stage III — the first OS improvement in this setting in decades.
Benefit was smallest in EGFR-mutant tumors (post hoc); LAURA now supplies osimertinib for that group.
trials.takeaway: Consolidation durvalumab after chemoradiation improves PFS and OS in unresectable stage III NSCLC

trials.name: FLAURA
trials.descriptor: first-line osimertinib vs 1st-gen TKI, metastatic EGFR+ NSCLC
trials.population: Treatment-naive advanced/metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 del or L858R (incl. stable CNS mets)
trials.arms: Osimertinib vs gefitinib or erlotinib
trials.results: PFS 18.9 vs 10.2 mo (HR 0.46); OS 38.6 vs 31.8 mo (HR 0.80, p=0.046); superior CNS control; less toxicity
trials.reference: Soria JC et al. NEJM 2018 (PFS); Ramalingam SS et al. NEJM 2020 (OS)
highlights: Made osimertinib the first-line standard for EGFR ex19del/L858R NSCLC (PFS + OS benefit over 1st-gen TKIs).
trials.takeaway: Osimertinib is the 1L standard for EGFR-mutant NSCLC (PFS and OS benefit over 1st-gen TKIs)

trials.name: KEYNOTE-189
trials.descriptor: pembrolizumab + pemetrexed/platinum vs chemotherapy, non-squamous NSCLC
trials.population: Untreated metastatic non-squamous NSCLC without EGFR/ALK alterations, any PD-L1
trials.arms: Pembrolizumab + pemetrexed + platinum × 4 → pembrolizumab + pemetrexed maintenance vs placebo + same chemo (crossover allowed)
trials.results: Primary: 12-mo OS 69.2% vs 49.4% (HR 0.49), PFS 8.8 vs 4.9 mo (HR 0.52); updated OS 22.0 vs 10.6 mo (HR 0.56), PFS 9.0 vs 4.9 mo (HR 0.49); benefit in all PD-L1 strata (TPS <1%: OS HR 0.52); 5-yr OS 19.4% vs 11.3%
trials.toxicity: Acute kidney injury 5.2% vs 0.5%; pneumonitis 4.4%
trials.reference: Gandhi L et al. NEJM 2018;378:2078; Garassino MC et al. JCO 2023 (5-yr)
highlights: Chemo-immunotherapy is the default first-line regimen for non-squamous NSCLC at any PD-L1 level (KEYNOTE-407 is the squamous counterpart).
For PD-L1 ≥50%, pembrolizumab alone (KEYNOTE-024) or with chemo are both acceptable; chemo adds response speed at the cost of toxicity.
trials.takeaway: Pembrolizumab + pemetrexed/platinum doubles OS in first-line non-squamous NSCLC regardless of PD-L1

trials.name: CheckMate 227
trials.descriptor: nivolumab + ipilimumab vs chemotherapy, first-line NSCLC
trials.population: Untreated stage IV or recurrent NSCLC without EGFR/ALK alterations; Part 1a PD-L1 ≥1%
trials.arms: Nivolumab 3 mg/kg q2wk + ipilimumab 1 mg/kg q6wk vs platinum doublet (vs nivolumab alone)
trials.primary_endpoint: OS in PD-L1 ≥1% (nivo + ipi vs chemo)
trials.results: OS 17.1 vs 14.9 mo (HR 0.79) in PD-L1 ≥1%; 5-yr OS 24% vs 14%; benefit also in PD-L1 <1% (OS 17.2 vs 12.2 mo)
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 treatment-related AEs 33% vs 36%; immune-mediated events (skin, endocrine, hepatic)
trials.reference: Hellmann MD et al. NEJM 2019;381:2020; Brahmer JR et al. JCO 2023 (5-yr)
highlights: Chemotherapy-free dual immunotherapy option for PD-L1 ≥1% NSCLC with durable 5-year survival — approved May 2020.
Low-dose ipilimumab (1 mg/kg q6wk) keeps toxicity comparable to chemo; CheckMate 9LA adds 2 cycles of chemo for faster control.
trials.takeaway: Nivolumab + low-dose ipilimumab improves OS over chemotherapy first-line in PD-L1 ≥1% NSCLC

trials.name: ADAURA
trials.descriptor: adjuvant osimertinib, resected stage IB–IIIA EGFR+ NSCLC
trials.population: Completely resected stage IB–IIIA NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 del or L858R, ± adjuvant chemotherapy
trials.arms: Osimertinib 80 mg daily × 3 years vs placebo
trials.results: DFS HR 0.20 (stage II–IIIA) — dramatic reduction in recurrence incl. CNS; 5-yr OS 88% vs 78% (HR 0.49)
trials.reference: Wu YL et al. NEJM 2020 (DFS); Tsuboi M et al. NEJM 2023 (OS)
highlights: Established 3 years of adjuvant osimertinib as standard for resected EGFR-mutant NSCLC — first targeted adjuvant therapy with an OS benefit.
trials.takeaway: 3 years of adjuvant osimertinib improves DFS and OS in resected EGFR-mutant NSCLC

trials.name: CROWN
trials.descriptor: lorlatinib vs crizotinib, first-line ALK-positive NSCLC
trials.population: Untreated advanced ALK-positive NSCLC (asymptomatic brain mets allowed)
trials.arms: Lorlatinib 100 mg daily vs crizotinib 250 mg BID
trials.results: 12-mo PFS 78% vs 39% (HR 0.28); 5-yr PFS 60% vs 8%, median not reached vs 9.1 mo (HR 0.19); intracranial ORR 82% vs 23%; time to CNS progression HR 0.06
trials.toxicity: Hyperlipidemia (majority), edema, weight gain, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects (cognitive/mood, ~40%)
trials.reference: Shaw AT et al. NEJM 2020;383:2018; Solomon BJ et al. JCO 2024 (5-yr)
highlights: Lorlatinib delivers the longest PFS ever reported for a targeted therapy in NSCLC — 60% progression-free at 5 years — and near-complete CNS protection.
Alectinib (ALEX) remains an alternative with a gentler toxicity profile; lorlatinib's CNS side effects require counseling.
trials.takeaway: First-line lorlatinib gives 60% 5-year PFS and near-complete CNS control in ALK+ NSCLC

trials.name: CheckMate 816
trials.descriptor: neoadjuvant nivolumab + chemotherapy, resectable NSCLC
trials.population: Resectable stage IB (≥4 cm)–IIIA NSCLC, no EGFR/ALK alterations
trials.arms: Nivolumab 360 mg + platinum doublet × 3 → surgery vs platinum doublet × 3 → surgery (no adjuvant IO)
trials.primary_endpoint: Event-free survival and pathologic complete response
trials.results: pCR 24.0% vs 2.2%; median EFS 31.6 vs 20.8 mo (HR 0.63); 5-yr OS 65% vs 55% (HR 0.72, 2025); surgery not delayed or compromised
trials.reference: Forde PM et al. NEJM 2022;386:1973; Spicer JD et al. NEJM 2025 (5-yr OS)
highlights: First approved neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy in NSCLC — three cycles before surgery, no adjuvant IO, with a 10-fold increase in pCR and an OS benefit.
pCR is a strong surrogate: patients with pCR have very few events.
trials.takeaway: Neoadjuvant nivolumab + chemo improves pCR, EFS and OS in resectable NSCLC

trials.name: AEGEAN
trials.descriptor: perioperative durvalumab, resectable NSCLC
trials.population: Resectable stage IIA–IIIB (N2) NSCLC without EGFR/ALK alterations
trials.arms: Durvalumab + platinum doublet × 4 → surgery → durvalumab × 12 vs placebo + chemo → surgery → placebo
trials.primary_endpoint: Event-free survival and pathologic complete response
trials.results: pCR 17.2% vs 4.3%; EFS HR 0.68 (12-mo 73.4% vs 64.5%); OS immature
trials.reference: Heymach JV et al. NEJM 2023;389:1672
highlights: Durvalumab's perioperative approval (FDA Aug 2024) — same design and similar effect size as KEYNOTE-671.
Choice among pembrolizumab, durvalumab and nivolumab perioperative regimens is largely institutional.
trials.takeaway: Perioperative durvalumab improves EFS and pCR in resectable NSCLC

trials.name: CALGB/Alliance 140503
trials.setting: Peripheral clinical T1aN0 NSCLC 2 cm or smaller
trials.descriptor: sublobar resection vs lobectomy for small peripheral node-negative NSCLC
trials.population: 697 patients with peripheral NSCLC clinically staged T1aN0 and 2 cm or smaller. Randomization occurred intraoperatively, only after nodal involvement was excluded by frozen section
trials.arms: Sublobar resection - wedge resection or segmentectomy, with wedge predominating - vs lobectomy
trials.results: DFS HR 1.01 (90% CI 0.83-1.24) - non-inferior. 5-year DFS 63.6% vs 64.1%; 5-year OS 80.3% vs 78.9% (OS HR 0.95). No difference in locoregional or distant recurrence
trials.toxicity: Pulmonary function at 6 months modestly favored sublobar resection. Perioperative morbidity and mortality were similar
trials.reference: Altorki N et al. N Engl J Med 2023;388:489-498
highlights: Overturned lobectomy as the automatic answer for small peripheral node-negative NSCLC, a standard that had stood since 1995
The intraoperative randomization matters: these patients had pathologically confirmed node-negative disease, so do not extrapolate to anyone staged radiographically alone
Read alongside JCOG0802, which found segmentectomy gave superior overall survival but doubled local relapse - the two trials used different operations and different endpoints
trials.takeaway: Sublobar resection is non-inferior to lobectomy for peripheral node-negative NSCLC 2 cm or smaller, after intraoperative nodal confirmation.

trials.name: FLAURA2
trials.descriptor: osimertinib + chemo vs osimertinib alone, first-line
trials.population: Treatment-naive advanced EGFR-mutant (ex19del/L858R) NSCLC
trials.arms: Osimertinib + platinum/pemetrexed vs osimertinib monotherapy
trials.results: PFS 25.5 vs 16.7 mo (HR 0.62); final OS 47.5 vs 37.6 mo (HR 0.77, p=0.02); more myelosuppression/toxicity
trials.reference: Planchard D et al. NEJM 2023 (PFS); NEJM 2025 (OS)
highlights: Adding chemo to osimertinib improves PFS and OS — favored for high-burden, CNS-metastatic, or L858R disease; monotherapy still reasonable when tolerability is the priority.
trials.takeaway: Osimertinib + platinum/pemetrexed improves PFS and OS over osimertinib alone in 1L EGFR-mutant NSCLC

trials.name: KEYNOTE-671
trials.descriptor: perioperative pembrolizumab (neoadjuvant + adjuvant), resectable NSCLC
trials.population: Resectable stage II–IIIB (N2) NSCLC, any PD-L1 (EGFR/ALK not required to be excluded but rare)
trials.arms: Pembrolizumab + cisplatin doublet × 4 → surgery → pembrolizumab × 13 vs placebo + chemo → surgery → placebo
trials.reference: Wakelee H et al. NEJM 2023;389:491; Spicer JD et al. Lancet 2024 (OS)
highlights: The perioperative model (neoadjuvant + adjuvant pembrolizumab) with an OS benefit — the reason KEYNOTE-671 is the most-cited among the perioperative trials (AEGEAN, CheckMate 77T, Neotorch).
Whether the adjuvant phase adds to neoadjuvant alone (CheckMate 816) is unresolved.
trials.takeaway: Perioperative pembrolizumab improves EFS and OS in resectable stage II–IIIB NSCLC

trials.name: LIBRETTO-431
trials.setting: Previously untreated advanced RET fusion-positive NSCLC
trials.descriptor: selpercatinib vs platinum chemotherapy with or without pembrolizumab in RET fusion-positive disease
trials.population: 261 patients with advanced RET fusion-positive NSCLC and no prior systemic therapy, randomized 2:1
trials.arms: Selpercatinib 160 mg PO twice daily vs investigator's choice of platinum-based chemotherapy with or without pembrolizumab
trials.primary_endpoint: Progression-free survival by blinded independent central review
trials.results: Median PFS 24.8 vs 11.2 months; HR 0.465 (95% CI 0.309-0.699), P<0.001. Intracranial ORR 82.4% vs 58.3%
trials.toxicity: Hypertension, transaminase elevation, QT prolongation, diarrhea. Generally more tolerable than chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab
trials.reference: Zhou C et al. N Engl J Med 2023;389:1839-1850
highlights: The only randomized frontline evidence in RET fusion-positive NSCLC - most driver approvals in this space rest on single-arm data
Beat chemo-IO, not just chemotherapy, which settles the question of whether a driver-positive patient should get immunotherapy first
Strong intracranial activity, relevant because RET fusion NSCLC has a high rate of brain metastases
trials.takeaway: Selpercatinib more than doubles progression-free survival versus chemotherapy with or without pembrolizumab in untreated RET fusion-positive NSCLC.

trials.name: PAPILLON
trials.setting: Previously untreated advanced NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertion
trials.descriptor: amivantamab plus chemotherapy as first-line therapy for EGFR exon 20 insertion disease
trials.population: 308 patients with advanced NSCLC harboring an EGFR exon 20 insertion, no prior systemic therapy for advanced disease
trials.arms: Amivantamab (weight-based) + carboplatin AUC 5 + pemetrexed 500 mg/m2, vs carboplatin + pemetrexed alone
trials.primary_endpoint: Progression-free survival by blinded independent central review
trials.results: Median PFS 11.4 vs 6.7 months; HR 0.40 (95% CI 0.30-0.53), P<0.001. ORR 73% vs 47%
trials.toxicity: Predominantly EGFR- and MET-related: rash, paronychia, hypoalbuminemia, infusion reactions. Venous thromboembolism is the notable risk - prophylactic anticoagulation for the first 4 months
trials.reference: Zhou C et al. N Engl J Med 2023;389:2039-2051
highlights: EGFR exon 20 insertions are resistant to osimertinib and the classic EGFR TKIs - this established the first effective frontline regimen
Contrast with mobocertinib, which was withdrawn worldwide in 2023 after EXCLAIM-2 missed its endpoint
Sunvozertinib is an option after platinum but carries only an accelerated, second-line-and-beyond approval
trials.takeaway: Amivantamab plus carboplatin-pemetrexed nearly doubles progression-free survival in untreated EGFR exon 20 insertion NSCLC and is the frontline standard.

trials.name: ALINA
trials.descriptor: adjuvant alectinib vs chemotherapy, resected ALK-positive NSCLC
trials.population: Completely resected stage IB (≥4 cm)–IIIA ALK-positive NSCLC
trials.arms: Alectinib 600 mg BID × 24 months vs platinum-based chemotherapy × 4
trials.results: DFS HR 0.24 (stage II–IIIA); 2-yr DFS 93.8% vs 63.0%; CNS DFS HR 0.22; OS immature
trials.reference: Wu YL et al. NEJM 2024;390:1265
highlights: Adjuvant alectinib × 2 years replaces chemotherapy for resected ALK-positive disease (FDA Apr 2024) — the ALK parallel to ADAURA.
Test ALK (and EGFR) on every resected non-squamous NSCLC before choosing adjuvant therapy; targeted agents preclude adjuvant IO.
trials.takeaway: 2 years of adjuvant alectinib dramatically improves DFS over chemotherapy in resected ALK+ NSCLC

trials.name: CheckMate 77T
trials.descriptor: perioperative nivolumab - neoadjuvant chemo-IO followed by adjuvant nivolumab
trials.population: 452 patients with resectable stage IIA-IIIB NSCLC, no EGFR or ALK alterations
trials.arms: Neoadjuvant nivolumab 360 mg + platinum doublet q3w x4 then surgery then adjuvant nivolumab 480 mg q4w x1 year, vs neoadjuvant placebo + chemotherapy then surgery then placebo
trials.results: EFS HR 0.58 (97.36% CI 0.42-0.81, P<0.001); 18-month EFS 70.2% vs 50.0%. pCR 25.3% vs 4.7%; major pathologic response 35.4% vs 12.1%
trials.toxicity: Grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events 32% vs 25%. Surgery was not delayed or cancelled more often in the nivolumab arm
trials.reference: Cascone T et al. N Engl J Med 2024;390:1756-1769
highlights: Completes the perioperative quartet alongside KEYNOTE-671 and AEGEAN, with EFS benefit of the same magnitude
Unlike CheckMate 816, which gave neoadjuvant therapy only, this continues IO after surgery - the perioperative-versus-neoadjuvant-only question is still unresolved
Do not use in EGFR- or ALK-altered disease
trials.takeaway: Perioperative nivolumab improves event-free survival in resectable NSCLC, matching the other perioperative chemo-IO regimens.

trials.name: LAURA
trials.descriptor: osimertinib after chemoradiation, unresectable stage III EGFR+ NSCLC
trials.population: Unresectable stage III EGFR-mutant (ex19del/L858R) NSCLC without progression after definitive chemoradiotherapy
trials.arms: Osimertinib until progression vs placebo (crossover to osimertinib at progression)
trials.results: PFS 39.1 vs 5.6 mo (HR 0.16, p<0.001); marked reduction in CNS + distant progression; OS immature (crossover)
trials.reference: Lu S et al. NEJM 2024; FDA approval Sept 2024
highlights: Replaced durvalumab consolidation in EGFR-mutant stage III disease — first phase 3 of a targeted agent after CRT.
trials.takeaway: Consolidation osimertinib after chemoRT in EGFR-mutant stage III NSCLC (PFS 39.1 vs 5.6 mo)

trials.name: MARIPOSA
trials.descriptor: amivantamab + lazertinib vs osimertinib, first-line EGFR-mutant NSCLC
trials.population: Untreated locally advanced/metastatic EGFR ex19del or L858R NSCLC
trials.arms: Amivantamab IV + lazertinib PO vs osimertinib vs lazertinib alone
trials.results: PFS 23.7 vs 16.6 mo (HR 0.70); OS HR 0.75 (median NR vs 36.7 mo, 2025); more toxicity
trials.toxicity: Rash, paronychia, infusion reactions, VTE (37% — prophylactic anticoagulation now recommended for the first 4 months), hypoalbuminemia
trials.reference: Cho BC et al. NEJM 2024;391:1486; Yang JCH et al. NEJM 2025 (OS)
highlights: The chemo-free intensification of first-line EGFR therapy — PFS and OS benefit over osimertinib at the cost of substantial dermatologic toxicity and VTE.
Competes with FLAURA2 (osimertinib + chemo); no head-to-head; subcutaneous amivantamab (PALOMA-3) eases delivery.
trials.takeaway: Amivantamab + lazertinib improves PFS and OS over osimertinib first-line in EGFR-mutant NSCLC, with more toxicity

trials.name: PRODIGE 4 / ACCORD 11
trials.descriptor: FOLFIRINOX vs gemcitabine in metastatic disease
trials.population: Metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, ECOG 0–1, age ≤75, bilirubin <1.5× ULN
trials.arms: FOLFIRINOX (oxaliplatin 85, irinotecan 180, LV, bolus + infusional 5-FU) q2wk vs gemcitabine weekly
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 neutropenia 45.7%, febrile neutropenia 5.4%, diarrhea 12.7%, neuropathy 9%
trials.reference: Conroy T et al. NEJM 2011;364:1817
highlights: First regimen to substantially beat gemcitabine — FOLFIRINOX is the reference first-line therapy for fit metastatic patients.
Strict eligibility (PS 0–1, normal bilirubin); modified FOLFIRINOX without bolus 5-FU is standard in practice.
trials.takeaway: FOLFIRINOX improves OS to 11.1 vs 6.8 months over gemcitabine in fit metastatic patients

trials.name: MPACT
trials.descriptor: gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel vs gemcitabine
trials.population: Metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, KPS ≥70 (broader eligibility than PRODIGE 4)
trials.arms: Nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m² + gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² d1, 8, 15 q4wk vs gemcitabine alone
trials.results: OS 8.5 vs 6.7 mo (HR 0.72); PFS 5.5 vs 3.7 mo; ORR 23% vs 7%
trials.toxicity: Neutropenia (38%), fatigue, neuropathy (17% grade ≥3, reversible)
trials.reference: Von Hoff DD et al. NEJM 2013;369:1691
highlights: Gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel is the first-line regimen for moderate performance status or when FOLFIRINOX is unsuitable.
Never compared head-to-head with FOLFIRINOX; the choice tracks fitness and toxicity preference.
trials.takeaway: Gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel improves OS over gemcitabine alone in metastatic pancreatic cancer

trials.name: ESPAC-4
trials.descriptor: adjuvant gemcitabine + capecitabine vs gemcitabine
trials.population: Resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (R0 or R1), within 12 weeks of surgery
trials.arms: Gemcitabine + capecitabine × 6 cycles vs gemcitabine alone
trials.results: OS 28.0 vs 25.5 mo (HR 0.82); 5-yr OS 28.8% vs 16.3%; benefit largest with R0 resection
trials.toxicity: Hand-foot syndrome and diarrhea added; similar grade 3–4 rates overall
trials.reference: Neoptolemos JP et al. Lancet 2017;389:1011
highlights: Gemcitabine + capecitabine is the adjuvant option for patients not fit for mFOLFIRINOX (modest 2.5-month median gain).
Never compared head-to-head with mFOLFIRINOX — the choice is made on performance status.
trials.takeaway: Adjuvant gemcitabine + capecitabine modestly improves OS over gemcitabine alone

trials.name: PRODIGE 24 / CCTG PA.6
trials.descriptor: adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX vs gemcitabine
trials.population: Resected pancreatic adenocarcinoma (R0/R1), ECOG 0–1, CA 19-9 <180, age ≤79, within 3–12 weeks of surgery
trials.arms: mFOLFIRINOX × 12 (irinotecan reduced to 150 mg/m², no bolus 5-FU) vs gemcitabine × 6 months
trials.toxicity: Grade 3–4 AEs 76% vs 53%: diarrhea, neuropathy, fatigue, neutropenia
trials.reference: Conroy T et al. NEJM 2018;379:2395; JAMA Oncol 2022 (5-yr)
highlights: Adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX is the standard for fit patients after resection — the longest median OS ever reported in resected PDAC.
Highly selected population (good PS, recovered from surgery); gemcitabine/capecitabine (ESPAC-4) for those who don't fit.
trials.takeaway: Adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX extends OS to 54 months vs 35 with gemcitabine in fit resected patients

trials.name: POLO
trials.descriptor: olaparib maintenance after platinum in germline BRCA-mutated metastatic disease
trials.population: Metastatic pancreatic cancer with germline BRCA1/2 mutation, no progression after ≥16 weeks of first-line platinum-based chemotherapy
trials.arms: Olaparib 300 mg BID maintenance vs placebo
trials.results: PFS 7.4 vs 3.8 mo (HR 0.53); 2-yr PFS 22.1% vs 9.6%; OS 19.0 vs 19.2 mo (NS)
trials.toxicity: Fatigue, nausea, anemia; grade ≥3 AEs 40% vs 23%
trials.reference: Golan T et al. NEJM 2019;381:317; JCO 2021 (OS)
highlights: Germline testing is indicated for all pancreatic cancer — a BRCA mutation opens platinum first-line and olaparib maintenance.
PFS benefit without OS benefit; a reasonable chemo-free maintenance option after platinum response.
trials.takeaway: Olaparib maintenance doubles PFS after platinum in germline BRCA-mutated metastatic pancreatic cancer

trials.name: KEYNOTE-158
trials.descriptor: pembrolizumab in previously treated MSI-H/dMMR non-colorectal solid tumors
trials.population: Advanced MSI-H/dMMR non-colorectal cancers after ≥1 prior therapy (27 tumor types; 22 pancreatic)
trials.arms: Single-arm: pembrolizumab 200 mg q3wk up to 2 years
trials.results: ORR 34.3% overall (CR 10%); median PFS 4.1 mo, OS 23.5 mo; pancreatic subgroup ORR 18.2%, median OS 4.0 mo
trials.reference: Marabelle A et al. JCO 2020;38:1
highlights: Supports the tissue-agnostic pembrolizumab approval for MSI-H/dMMR tumors — MSI-H pancreatic cancer is rare (~1%) and responds less than other sites.
Also the basis for pembrolizumab in TMB ≥10 mut/Mb solid tumors (separate cohort analysis).
trials.takeaway: Pembrolizumab yields durable responses in refractory MSI-H/dMMR tumors across sites (ORR 34%), lower in pancreatic

trials.name: NAPOLI-3
trials.descriptor: NALIRIFOX vs gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel
trials.population: Untreated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, ECOG 0–1
trials.arms: NALIRIFOX (liposomal irinotecan 50 + oxaliplatin 60 + LV + 5-FU 2400 q2wk) vs gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel
trials.toxicity: Diarrhea (20% grade ≥3), nausea, hypokalemia; less neutropenia and neuropathy than gem/nab-P
trials.reference: Wainberg ZA et al. Lancet 2023;402:1272
highlights: First head-to-head win of a fluoropyrimidine/irinotecan/oxaliplatin triplet over gem/nab-paclitaxel; FDA-approved Feb 2024.
No direct comparison with FOLFIRINOX; median OS numbers are near-identical and NALIRIFOX costs far more.
trials.takeaway: NALIRIFOX improves OS over gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel first-line (11.1 vs 9.2 mo)

trials.name: EORTC 22863
trials.descriptor: radiotherapy ± 3 years of ADT, locally advanced disease
trials.population: T3–T4 any grade, or T1–T2 WHO grade 3, N0–1 M0 prostate cancer
trials.arms: RT (70 Gy) + goserelin × 3 years (started with RT) vs RT alone (ADT at relapse)
trials.results: 5-yr OS 79% vs 62%; 10-yr OS 58.1% vs 39.8% (HR 0.60); 10-yr clinical DFS 47.7% vs 22.7%; prostate cancer mortality 10.3% vs 30.4%
trials.reference: Bolla M et al. NEJM 1997;337:295; Bolla M et al. Lancet Oncol 2010;11:1066 (10-yr)
highlights: The foundational trial for long-term ADT with radiation in high-risk/locally advanced disease — an 18-point OS gain at 10 years.
Defined the 3-year ADT standard that later trials (22961, PCS IV, DART) tried to shorten.
trials.takeaway: 3 years of ADT with radiation dramatically improves OS in locally advanced prostate cancer

trials.name: RTOG 9202
trials.setting: Locally advanced, short vs long ADT
trials.descriptor: 4 months vs 28 months of ADT with radiation
trials.population: T2c–T4 N0–Nx prostate cancer, PSA <150
trials.arms: RT + 4 months neoadjuvant/concurrent ADT vs the same + 24 additional months of goserelin (28 months total)
trials.results: 5-yr OS 80.0% vs 78.5% (NS); Gleason 8–10 5-yr OS 81.0% vs 70.7%. 10-yr: DFS 22.5% vs 13.2%; disease-specific survival 88.7% vs 83.9%; OS 53.9% vs 51.6% (NS overall) but Gleason 8–10 OS 45.1% vs 31.9% (p=0.0061)
trials.reference: Hanks GE et al. JCO 2003;21:3972; Horwitz EM et al. JCO 2008;26:2497 (10-yr)
highlights: Long-term ADT improves disease control for locally advanced disease; the OS benefit is concentrated in Gleason 8–10.
Supports the long-course standard alongside EORTC 22961 and DART.
trials.takeaway: Extending ADT from 4 to 28 months with RT improves DFS, and OS in Gleason 8–10 disease

trials.name: TAX 327
trials.descriptor: docetaxel vs mitoxantrone
trials.population: 1,006 men with mCRPC
trials.arms: Docetaxel 75 mg/m2 q3wk vs docetaxel 30 mg/m2 weekly vs mitoxantrone 12 mg/m2 q3wk, all + prednisone
trials.results: Median OS 18.9 vs 17.4 vs 16.5 mo; q3wk docetaxel vs mitoxantrone HR 0.76 (0.62-0.94), P=0.009; weekly HR 0.91, NS. PSA response 45% / 48% / 32%
trials.reference: Tannock IF et al. N Engl J Med 2004;351:1502-1512
highlights: First chemotherapy to prolong survival in mCRPC
Every-3-week schedule, not weekly, carried the survival benefit
Still the backbone taxane for mCRPC
trials.takeaway: Docetaxel every 3 weeks with prednisone was the first therapy to improve survival in mCRPC.

trials.name: EORTC 22961
trials.setting: Locally advanced, 6 mo vs 3 yr ADT
trials.descriptor: 6 months vs 3 years of ADT with radiation, locally advanced disease
trials.population: T1c–T2b N1–2 or T2c–T4 N0–2 M0 prostate cancer (locally advanced)
trials.arms: RT + 6 months ADT vs RT + 3 years ADT (non-inferiority)
trials.results: 5-yr overall mortality 19.0% vs 15.2% (OS 81.0% vs 84.8%; HR 1.42 for short-term) — 6 months NOT non-inferior; prostate cancer deaths 47 vs 29 (4.7% vs 3.2%)
trials.reference: Bolla M et al. NEJM 2009;360:2516
highlights: Six months of ADT is not enough for high-risk/locally advanced disease treated with RT — long-course (18–36 months) remains standard.
RTOG 9202 and DART 01/05 reached the same conclusion, especially in Gleason 8–10.
trials.takeaway: 6 months of ADT is inferior to 3 years with radiation for locally advanced prostate cancer

trials.name: TROPIC
trials.descriptor: cabazitaxel vs mitoxantrone
trials.population: 755 men with mCRPC progressing after docetaxel
trials.arms: Cabazitaxel 25 mg/m2 vs mitoxantrone 12 mg/m2 q3wk, each + prednisone
trials.toxicity: Grade >=3 neutropenia 82% vs 58%; febrile neutropenia 8% vs 1%; diarrhea 6%
trials.reference: de Bono JS et al. Lancet 2010;376:1147-1154
highlights: Established cabazitaxel post-docetaxel
High neutropenia rates led to G-CSF prophylaxis and the 20 mg/m2 dose (PROSELICA)
Precursor to CARD
trials.takeaway: Cabazitaxel improves survival over mitoxantrone after docetaxel in mCRPC.

trials.name: RTOG 9408
trials.descriptor: radiotherapy ± 4 months of ADT, mostly intermediate-risk localized disease
trials.population: T1b–T2b prostate cancer, PSA ≤20 (mostly intermediate risk; 35% low risk)
trials.arms: RT (66.6 Gy) + 4 months of ADT (2 months neoadjuvant + 2 concurrent) vs RT alone
trials.results: 10-yr OS 62% vs 57% (HR 1.17 for RT alone); disease-specific mortality 4% vs 8%; benefit confined to intermediate-risk disease (10-yr OS 61% vs 54%), none in low risk
trials.reference: Jones CU et al. NEJM 2011;365:107
highlights: Established short-course (4–6 month) ADT with radiation for intermediate-risk disease; low-risk patients gain nothing from ADT.
Modern dose-escalated RT and favorable/unfavorable intermediate-risk splits refine who still needs it (favorable intermediate: RT alone is reasonable).
trials.takeaway: 4 months of ADT with radiation improves OS in intermediate-risk, not low-risk, localized prostate cancer

trials.name: ALSYMPCA
trials.descriptor: radium-223, mCRPC with symptomatic bone metastases
trials.population: mCRPC with symptomatic bone metastases, no known visceral metastases
trials.arms: Radium-223 (50 kBq/kg IV q4wk ×6) vs placebo, both + best standard of care
trials.results: OS 14.9 vs 11.3 mo (HR 0.70, p<0.001); time to first symptomatic skeletal event 15.6 vs 9.8 mo
trials.reference: Parker C et al. NEJM 2013;369:213
highlights: First alpha emitter to improve OS in prostate cancer.
Bone-only agent — a calcium mimetic with no activity against visceral or nodal disease.
Alpha particles have a very short tissue range → potent local effect with limited marrow toxicity.
trials.takeaway: Radium-223 improves OS in mCRPC with symptomatic bone-only metastases

trials.name: CHAARTED
trials.descriptor: docetaxel added to ADT in metastatic castration-sensitive disease
trials.population: Metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer (M1 CSPC)
trials.arms: ADT + docetaxel 75 mg/m² q3wk ×6 vs ADT alone
trials.results: OS 57.6 vs 44.0 mo (HR 0.61, p<0.001); benefit concentrated in high-volume disease (49.2 vs 32.2 mo)
trials.reference: Sweeney CJ et al. NEJM 2015;373:737
highlights: Established chemo-hormonal therapy — the first proof that ADT alone is not enough in M1 CSPC.
Defined high-volume disease: visceral metastases, or ≥4 bone lesions with ≥1 beyond the axial skeleton — a definition still used to pick triplet therapy.
trials.takeaway: ADT + docetaxel improves OS in M1 CSPC, mostly in high-volume disease

trials.name: DART 01/05 GICOR
trials.setting: Intermediate/high-risk, 4 vs 28 mo ADT with dose-escalated RT
trials.descriptor: short vs long ADT with high-dose (≥76 Gy) radiotherapy
trials.population: Intermediate- and high-risk localized prostate cancer (T1c–T3b N0 M0), treated with dose-escalated 3D-conformal RT
trials.arms: 4 months ADT vs 28 months ADT (goserelin), both with RT ≥76 Gy
trials.results: 5-yr bDFS 90% vs 81% (HR 1.88 for short-term); 5-yr OS 95% vs 86% (HR 2.48); benefit driven by high-risk patients (bDFS 88% vs 76%, OS 96% vs 82%)
trials.reference: Zapatero A et al. Lancet Oncol 2015;16:320
highlights: Shows long-course ADT still matters even with dose-escalated radiation — high-dose RT does not substitute for ADT duration in high-risk disease.
The 10-year update (2022) retained the high-risk benefit but not the OS difference overall.
trials.takeaway: 28 months of ADT beats 4 months even with dose-escalated RT in high-risk localized prostate cancer

trials.name: LATITUDE
trials.descriptor: abiraterone added to ADT in high-risk M1 CSPC
trials.population: Newly diagnosed high-risk M1 CSPC (≥2 of: Gleason ≥8, ≥3 bone lesions, visceral metastases)
trials.arms: ADT + abiraterone/prednisone vs ADT + placebo
trials.results: 3-yr OS 66% vs 49% (HR 0.62); rPFS 33.0 vs 14.8 mo
trials.reference: Fizazi K et al. NEJM 2017;377:352
highlights: First androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor to show survival benefit in M1 CSPC, opening the door to non-chemo intensification.
trials.takeaway: ADT + abiraterone improves OS in high-risk M1 CSPC

trials.name: RTOG 9601
trials.descriptor: salvage RT +/- 24 months of bicalutamide
trials.population: 760 men with rising PSA after radical prostatectomy (pT2 with positive margin or pT3)
trials.arms: Salvage RT + bicalutamide 150 mg daily x 24 mo vs RT + placebo
trials.results: 12-yr OS 76.3% vs 71.3%, HR 0.77 (0.59-0.99), P=0.04. 12-yr prostate cancer death 5.8% vs 13.4%; metastases 14.5% vs 23.0%
trials.toxicity: Gynecomastia 69.7% vs 10.9%
trials.reference: Shipley WU et al. N Engl J Med 2017;376:417-428
highlights: First trial showing hormone therapy with salvage RT improves survival
Benefit concentrated at higher pre-RT PSA in secondary analyses
Bicalutamide 150 mg is now often replaced by short-course LHRH ADT (SPPORT)
trials.takeaway: Adding 2 years of bicalutamide to salvage RT improves overall survival after prostatectomy.

trials.name: Low-dose abiraterone with food (Szmulewitz)
trials.descriptor: abiraterone 250 mg with a low-fat meal vs 1000 mg fasting
trials.population: 72 men with mCRPC
trials.arms: Abiraterone 250 mg with low-fat breakfast vs 1000 mg fasting, each + prednisone 5 mg BID
trials.primary_endpoint: Log change in PSA at 12 weeks (non-inferiority)
trials.results: Log PSA change -1.59 (low dose) vs -1.19 (standard); non-inferiority met. PSA response 58% vs 50%; median PFS ~9 months in both arms
trials.reference: Szmulewitz RZ et al. J Clin Oncol 2018;36:1389-1395
highlights: Food markedly increases abiraterone absorption - one quarter of the dose with a low-fat meal gives equivalent PSA effect
Small phase 2 with a PSA endpoint - no survival data
A practical option when cost is a barrier
trials.takeaway: Abiraterone 250 mg with a low-fat meal is non-inferior to 1000 mg fasting on PSA response.

trials.name: PCS IV
trials.descriptor: 18 vs 36 months of ADT with radiation, high-risk localized disease
trials.population: High-risk localized prostate cancer (T3–T4, or PSA >20, or Gleason >7)
trials.arms: RT + 18 months ADT vs RT + 36 months ADT
trials.results: 5-yr OS 86% (18 mo) vs 91% (36 mo), p=0.07; 10-yr OS 62% vs 62% (HR 1.02); disease-specific survival 87% vs 87%; quality of life favored 18 months (6 scales, 13 items)
trials.reference: Nabid A et al. Eur Urol 2018;74:432
highlights: 18 months of ADT is as effective as 36 months for high-risk disease treated with RT — the practical upper bound in most guidelines.
Combined with the 2026 meta-analysis (benefit plateaus after ~12 months), the trend is toward the shorter end of 18–36 months.
trials.takeaway: 18 months of ADT with radiation is equivalent to 36 months in high-risk localized prostate cancer

trials.name: PRECISION
trials.descriptor: MRI with targeted biopsy vs standard TRUS biopsy
trials.population: 500 biopsy-naive men with suspected prostate cancer
trials.arms: Multiparametric MRI with targeted biopsy only if suspicious (no biopsy if negative) vs standard 10-12-core TRUS biopsy
trials.results: Clinically significant cancer 38% vs 26% (adjusted difference 12 points, P=0.005); clinically insignificant cancer 13 points lower (P<0.001); 28% of MRI arm avoided biopsy
trials.reference: Kasivisvanathan V et al. N Engl J Med 2018;378:1767-1777
highlights: Established MRI-first diagnostic pathway
Detects more significant and fewer insignificant cancers
Over a quarter avoid biopsy altogether
trials.takeaway: MRI-targeted biopsy detects more clinically significant and fewer insignificant cancers than standard TRUS biopsy.

trials.name: PROSPER
trials.descriptor: enzalutamide in non-metastatic CRPC
trials.population: M0 CRPC with PSA doubling time ≤10 months
trials.arms: Enzalutamide 160 mg daily vs placebo, both + ADT
trials.results: MFS 36.6 vs 14.7 mo (HR 0.29). Final OS (Sternberg CN et al. NEJM 2020;382:2197): 67.0 vs 56.3 mo, HR 0.73 (0.61-0.89), P=0.001
trials.reference: Hussain M et al. NEJM 2018;378:2465; final OS Sternberg CN et al. NEJM 2020;382:2197
highlights: Second of the "MFS trio" (SPARTAN / PROSPER / ARAMIS) — all roughly doubled metastasis-free survival.
Overall survival benefit confirmed at final analysis (OS HR 0.69-0.78 across the three nmCRPC trials)
